checks.check: Every fact has a source URL and date
No invented quotes, statistics or real weddings

facts.claim: Hymnary.org lists 'Be Thou my vision, O Lord of my heart' with versifier Eleanor Henrietta Hull and translator Mary E. Byrne (1905), sung to the tune SLANE.

Hymnary.org's worship notes say the source is an Irish poem attributed to the monk Dallan Forgaill, translated into English by Mary Elizabeth Byrne in the early 20th century and versified by Eleanor Hull in 1912; one hymnal instance gives the source as 'Irish, c. 8th century'.
Hymnary.org says SLANE is an old Irish folk tune, arranged by David Evans and set to 'Be Thou My Vision' in the Church Hymnary (1927).
Hymnary.org lists 'Amazing grace! (how sweet the sound)' by John Newton (1779), sung to the tune NEW BRITAIN.
Hymnary.org says Newton published the hymn in 1779 in the Olney Hymns, a collaboration with William Cowper, under the original title 'Faith's Review and Expectations'.
Hymnary.org describes NEW BRITAIN (also known as AMAZING GRACE) as an Appalachian folk tune that first appeared in Southern Harmony; the modern harmonisation is credited to Edwin Othello Excell.
Hymnary.org lists 'Joyful, joyful, we adore Thee' by Henry Van Dyke (1907), sung to the tune HYMN TO JOY.
facts.conflicts: Hymnary.org header dates the text 1907; its worship notes say 'around 1908'. Use 1907 (header) or 'early 1900s'.

facts.claim: Hymnary.org says HYMN TO JOY (ODE TO JOY) adapts the final movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony as a congregational melody, and that Van Dyke wrote his text to be sung to Beethoven's 'Hymn to Joy'.
Hymnary.org gives the tune's meter as 87.87.D.

insider_details.detail: Amazing Grace is short in common meter and Hymnary.org notes most hymnals print four of Newton's stanzas plus a later anonymous fifth; for a ceremony, agree with the musician which verses to sing so the hymn fits the signing or a reflection moment.

Joyful, Joyful, We Adore Thee uses Beethoven's Ode to Joy melody, so it works for guests who don't know hymns: they will recognise the tune even if the words are new. Print the words in the order of service.

Be Thou My Vision is sung to an Irish folk tune (SLANE), which suits couples wanting an Irish or Celtic thread in a church ceremony, and is often played slowly; ask the musician to keep the tempo moving so it doesn't drag.
